title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Commercial and office cleaning
audience: Owners of small commercial and office cleaning businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting a building, a tenant or a facilities manager.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with the vendor range and local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits and one-off call-outs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on the type of building, the standard the client specifies, after-hours access, how often the crew visits and the cost of running the business. A crew that can clean several buildings on one route may justify a rate that protects its travel time, while a one-off clean across town needs more margin. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly, rather than cutting it to win work. For a sense check, Clean Group gives $35 to $65 per hour for most office and business premises, with a 2026 national average of about $45 to $55, and gives Sydney standard office at $50 to $65 and Melbourne at $48 to $62 (updated 15 March 2026). That is a figure from a company that sells cleaning services, so use it to check your rate, not to set it.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between buildings, waiting for after-hours access, lift booking, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. For example, if sixty of every hundred paid hours are billable, the costs of all one hundred hours must be recovered from the sixty, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, and its example gives 1,344 billable hours a year for 40 hours a week at 70 per cent (published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026). The page does not show its working weeks, and the range is not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (page metadata dated 1 October 2026). Labour on-costs such as payroll tax, workers' compensation, training and unpaid travel can add 25 to 40 per cent on top of wages, and Jobber says cleaners often undercount them (31 March 2026). That is a US-leaning guide, and payroll tax and workers' compensation are set state by state, so use your own state's figures. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. Xero's worked example shows the method: $93,000 to earn before tax, 46 working weeks and 25 billable hours in a 38-hour week give about $81 an hour (3 September 2026). That example is not a cleaning business. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for the owner before the rate is published. Compare your labour share of turnover with the ATO benchmark range for your own industry (last updated 17 March 2025), and review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: Short visits can cost more in time than they earn, because travel and set-up do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge covers the time needed to attend the site and start work. Cleaners either set a two- or three-hour minimum or a flat minimum. Jobber gives $100 as an example flat minimum and notes that a 30-minute job at $50 an hour leaves little profit after driving and overhead. A contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin. Its figures are labelled illustrative, so use the method only: a $105 visit cost at a 30 per cent target margin gives a $150 minimum (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). When several small tasks are done in one visit, price them as one labour amount rather than stacking a separate minimum for each task. State the minimum in writing before the visit.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate, then compare it with the vendor range.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit or call-out, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only. An owner needs $60,000 a year from billable work. The owner pays for 2,000 hours a year, but only 1,200 of them (60 per cent) can be billed to a building. The owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What rate does each method produce, what does the business earn at the wrong rate, and what should be checked before the rate is published?
workedExamples.reasoning: Built from billable hours, the rate is $60,000 divided by 1,200, which is $50 an hour. Built from all paid hours, the rate is $30 an hour, which looks lower and seems cheaper to the client. But only 1,200 hours can be sold, so $30 an hour brings in $36,000 and leaves a $24,000 gap. The rate must be built from billable hours. Then check it against the vendor range of $35 to $65 an hour for most office premises (Clean Group, updated 15 March 2026), the owner's own costs, the minimum charge and the tax treatment of leave and superannuation.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking your costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with the vendor range and local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking one-off short visits at the same rate, without covering travel, set-up and admin.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC's pricing guidance (last modified 15 July 2026) says misleading statements about prices are prohibited. The research file does not confirm whether that guidance covers minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term, so check those points before publishing a price sheet. A contract term that lets one party alone change prices may be unfair, and the ACCC's small business guide (July 2021, an older source) warns of this, so check any rate-change clause in a multi-year commercial contract.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation for the owner with a registered tax agent before publishing the rate. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with the vendor range and local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit or call-out.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against the vendor range and local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits and call-outs.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with the vendor range and local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. Supports: billable time about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours; 40 hours at 70 per cent gives 1,344 billable hours a year. General range, not Australian.

Jobber, 'How Much to Charge for House Cleaning', https://getjobber.com/academy/cleaning/how-much-to-charge-for-house-cleaning/, dated 31 March 2026. Supports: labour on-costs of 25 to 40 per cent; two- or three-hour or flat minimums; $100 example flat minimum. US-leaning source.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: the rate built from take-home pay, business costs and super, divided by billable hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, dated 23 September 2026. Figures labelled illustrative; method only. Supports: minimum set from full visit cost; several small tasks priced as one labour amount.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

ATO, 'Types of small business benchmarks', https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/small-business-benchmarks/types-of-benchmarks, last updated 17 March 2025. Supports: compare labour share with the range for your own industry. No trade figures taken.

Clean Group, 'Commercial cleaning pricing guide', https://www.clean-group.com.au/how-much-does-workplace-cleaning-cost-in-australia, updated 15 March 2026. Vendor source. Supports: $35 to $65 per hour for most office premises; Sydney and Melbourne standard office ranges.

ACCC, 'Small business and the Competition and Consumer Act', https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/Small%20business%20and%20the%20Competition%20and%20Consumer%20Act%20-%20July%202021.pdf, July 2021 (older source). Supports: a term that lets one party alone change prices may be unfair. Legal note, not pricing guidance.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.
